I would keep my land in the usual Quzhou pattern: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same fields. I am in south Hebei on the North China Plain, so this rotation fits my weather, my machinery, and how water comes here. The wheat is already in the ground at the start of the season, and I would push it through harvest in June because wheat is still the safer cash-and-grain crop for me. After that, I would go straight into summer maize because the summer rain matches maize much better than it matches wheat, and I can use the same land twice in one year. I would not spread myself across too many crops. Cotton and other cash crops can bring opportunity, but they also bring more labor, more management risk, and more market uncertainty. I would rather run a simpler system that I know well and can manage tightly.

On fertilizer, I would stay moderate instead of chasing maximum input. In my place, too much nitrogen is easy to waste, especially on wheat, and irrigation water is too valuable to farm loosely. I would use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed because that is where I trust the return most. I would irrigate wheat more than maize, since wheat grows through the dry season here, while maize can lean more on summer rainfall. For tillage, I would use rotary tillage ahead of wheat because it is practical and familiar for seedbed preparation, and I would seed maize with no-tillage after wheat harvest to save time and moisture. I would keep pesticide use limited to what I expect I will need for common weed, disease, and insect pressure rather than spraying blindly. I am aiming for stable yield, controlled cost, and a season I can manage with confidence.
